# x86_avx.py cases where Rosetta and an x86 CPU differ: what it left (docs/macos/avx-data/silicon_overrides.py writes this file). One corpus line per family run on the x86 CPU, an AMD EPYC 9V74 (raven-macos-bench run 44505811968, assembled with clang as here; dump sha256 28aa394685cacc237ca24c7a37fd3ed396d7f0918d4b4222fa5010879a1bf28b): the tests refuse the file when a family's cases or Rosetta's results change.
# The avx2 broadcast family: an AMD EPYC 7763 (run 44508125477), which agrees with Rosetta in all 100. Earlier runs: an AMD EPYC 9V74 (run 44505099547, all but the gathers), AMD EPYC 7763 (runs 44501136642, 44503053255) and 9V74 (44499294363, 44502534716) gave the same results for the families they had. Intel Xeon Platinum 8370C (run 44500206597) and 8573C (run 44503360598): they agree with Rosetta in the strings family, as the EPYCs do; the 8573C agrees with Rosetta in all 600 approximation cases, where the EPYCs differ in 358, and with the EPYC in the 8 fma addsub MXCSR values; both differ from the AMD runs in one dpps case (#7786, NaN lanes), not applied here: the AMD EPYC stays the reference.
# The strings wide and shift counts families: an Intel Xeon Platinum 8573C (run 44510983438, dump sha256 d4f8cd7d19083f3abb868f89bc1bf99c912f504e0bcb4c43c46c41b8d891619e), no AMD runner came up; it agrees with Rosetta in all 400 strings wide cases and differs in 112 shift counts cases, where Rosetta shifts a quadword by the low 32 bits of its count.
